title: Where's My Driver
hook: Your ride-hailing app has 1 million active drivers, and each one sends a GPS ping every 4 seconds. Riders want to see nearby cars instantly and watch their driver move on the map.
context: Ride-hailing location pipeline: ingestion, nearby search, and live tracking.
solution_brief: Compute the write rate first (250k per second), store only latest positions hot with TTL, index by geospatial cells with neighbour queries, and push targeted updates with client interpolation. 1M drivers divided by 4s is 250,000 writes per second. Latest position in memory with TTL, history on a stream. Geohash, S2 or H3 cells with neighbour lookups. Move cell membership as drivers cross boundaries. Targeted push plus client interpolation for tracking.

steps.prompt: A million drivers each send a GPS ping every 4 seconds. Which option gives the right write rate and a storage design that fits it?

options.text: About 1,000 writes per second, so any database copes
About 250,000 writes per second: latest positions in memory, history on a stream
About 250,000 writes per second: insert every ping as a durable row in a single relational table
About 4 million writes per second: impractical, so sample 1 driver in 16

steps.explanation: One million divided by 4 seconds is 250,000 updates per second. Matching needs only the latest position, so an in-memory store with a separate stream for history fits, whereas one durable row per ping in a single table is a risky fit for that rate without partitioning and load tests. Sampling drivers would leave most of the fleet invisible.
steps.bottleneck_note: Calculate ingest rate first, then separate latest-state reads from historical storage.

steps.prompt: Matching a rider to a driver needs only where each driver is now. How should the hot path store positions?
steps.context_note: Most of those 250,000 writes per second are obsolete the moment the next ping arrives.

options.text: Keep every ping in the hot store permanently
Ask each driver app for its position only when a rider requests a ride
Keep only the latest position per driver, with a TTL for silent drivers
Keep the latest position per driver with no expiry and clean up in a nightly job

steps.explanation: The hot path needs current state, which overwrites itself, and a TTL removes drivers who stop reporting without any cleanup job. Stream history for trips and disputes separately. Keeping every ping hot is costly and slows the queries that matter, and asking on demand makes every ride request wait on a phone.
steps.bottleneck_note: Separate current state (small, hot) from history (large, cold).

steps.prompt: A rider requests a car. How do you find drivers within 2 km without comparing the rider to all 1,000,000?
steps.context_note: Each ride request is currently compared against every driver.

options.text: Scan every driver and compute the distance to each
Index drivers by city only, then scan every driver in that city for each request
Reuse the result of the rider's last search for ten minutes
Index drivers by geospatial cell and rank the rider's cell and its neighbours

steps.explanation: A cell index (geohash, S2 or H3) turns a global search into a local one, so the cost follows the number of drivers in a few cells rather than the whole fleet. A city-level index still leaves tens or hundreds of thousands of drivers to scan, and a cached result is out of date as soon as cars move.
steps.bottleneck_note: Index by location so the search cost scales with local density, not total size.

steps.prompt: A rider near a cell edge sees no cars although one is 100 metres away across the boundary, and a driver who crossed into a new cell is listed in both. Which change fixes both problems?

options.text: Query neighbouring cells too, and move drivers between cells on each update
Shrink the cells to about one metre across so that cell boundaries rarely matter
Widen the search to the whole city whenever the rider's own cell is empty
Remove the driver from the old cell only when its entry expires

steps.explanation: A nearby driver can sit just across a boundary, so the query must cover adjacent cells, and membership has to follow the driver or stale entries linger, with a TTL cleaning up anything missed. Metre-wide cells would explode the number of cells to query, and relying on expiry alone leaves drivers in two cells for the whole TTL.
steps.bottleneck_note: Spatial indexes create edge cases at their borders. Query neighbours and move members.

steps.prompt: How should live tracking be delivered to those riders?
steps.context_note: Once a ride is booked, 200,000 riders are each polling for their driver's position every second.

options.text: Keep every rider polling once a second, and add more API servers to cope
Push updates only to the tracking rider over a persistent connection
Broadcast every driver's position to every rider's app
Send the position once at booking and refresh only when the rider taps the map

steps.explanation: Only the booked rider needs a given driver's updates, so a targeted push replaces 200,000 constant polls, and client-side interpolation keeps motion smooth at a lower update rate. Broadcasting everything to everyone wastes bandwidth and exposes driver locations, and refresh-on-tap defeats the point of live tracking.
steps.bottleneck_note: Send each update only to those who need it, and let the client smooth the gaps.
